title: Judges 9:50–57
context: At Thebez, Abimelech captures the city, but its people shelter in a strong tower. As he approaches the door to burn it, a woman drops an upper millstone on his head. Mortally wounded, he has his armor bearer kill him so it will not be said that a woman killed him. The narrator closes the story by stating that God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech and of the men of Shechem, and that Jotham’s curse came on them.

verses.text: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez, and took it.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech moves to Thebez, encamps, and takes it. Arminian readers note that the text gives no reason for this attack, suggesting that his violence now spreads beyond Shechem to other towns in the region.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his campaign as overreach that will lead to his downfall. Both traditions acknowledge that Thebez is sometimes linked with a site northeast of Shechem, though the identification is not certain.

verses.text: But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled there, and shut themselves in, and went up to the roof of the tower.
verses.arminianNotes: A strong tower stands within the city, and all its people flee there and go up to the roof. Arminian readers note the parallel with the tower of Shechem, as frightened people again seek refuge from Abimelech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated situation as setting up a reversal: this time the outcome will be different. Shared ground: the scene invites comparison with 9:46–49, with readers expecting another burning that does not come.

verses.text: Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it, and came near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech approaches the tower door to burn it. Arminian readers note that he repeats his earlier tactic, confident in his success, and comes close to the door where he becomes exposed to those above.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a man whose cruelty has become routine, now drawing near to the judgment he cannot see coming. Both traditions read his approach as a moment of tension that turns the story from repeated violence to sudden reversal.

verses.text: A certain woman cast an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, and broke his skull.
verses.arminianNotes: A woman drops an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head and breaks his skull. Arminian readers note that one unnamed woman ends his reign of terror, and that this event was remembered later in Israel (2 Samuel 11:21).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment arriving through an ordinary household tool in the hands of an unnamed person. Shared ground: the man who killed his brothers on one stone is struck down by a stone, a reversal the narrative leaves for readers to notice.

verses.text: Then he called hastily to the young man, his armor bearer, and said to him, “Draw your sword and kill me, that men not say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’ His young man thrust him through, and he died.”
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech has his armor bearer kill him so no one will say a woman killed him. Arminian readers see his pride enduring to the last moment. His concern is reputation, not repentance, even as he dies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that his attempt to avoid shame fails, since the story is remembered for the woman’s act. Both traditions see a contrast with Saul’s request to his armor bearer (1 Samuel 31:4), where the circumstances and outcome differ.

verses.text: When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they each departed to his place.
verses.arminianNotes: When the men of Israel see that Abimelech is dead, they go home. Arminian readers note the abrupt end of his followers’ loyalty, which depended on his power rather than on any lasting cause or calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the quiet dispersal as showing that his kingship had no foundation in God’s call. Shared ground: the men of Israel simply return home, and Israel’s first experiment with a king ends without ceremony or succession.

verses.text: Thus God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did to his father in killing his seventy brothers;
verses.arminianNotes: God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech for killing his seventy brothers. Arminian readers stress that God judges the free choices of moral agents, and see Abimelech’s death as the just consequence of his crime.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God governed all these events to bring about just repayment. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the narrator interprets the whole story as God’s righteous judgment on bloodshed, even through the actions of sinful people.

verses.text: and God repaid all the wickedness of the men of Shechem on their heads; and the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal came on them.
verses.arminianNotes: God repaid the men of Shechem, and Jotham’s curse came on them. Arminian readers note that the people who supported Abimelech are held fully accountable for their part, and that the curse took effect through their own conflicts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of Jotham’s words as confirming God’s faithfulness to the cause of the innocent. Both traditions read the closing verses as the narrator’s explicit theological verdict on the entire chapter.
